title: Competition is for Losers: why startups should aim for monopoly and avoid competition
summary: Thiel argues value creation (X) and value capture (Y%) are independent, so industries like airlines create huge value but capture almost none. There are only two kinds of businesses, perfectly competitive ones and monopolies, and people lie about which they are. Start in a small market, build durable monopoly traits, and aim to be the last mover.

principles.text: A valuable company both creates value and captures a share of it; the two variables are independent.
principles.quote: X and Y are completely independent variables and so um X can be very Big Y can be very small

principles.text: There are really just two kinds of businesses, perfect competition and monopoly, with almost nothing in between.
principles.quote: there are exactly two kinds of businesses in this world there are businesses that are perfectly competitive and there are businesses that are monopolies

principles.text: Monopolists and competitors both lie about their markets: monopolists claim a huge market, competitors claim a tiny unique one.
principles.quote: the basic lie you tell as a non-m monopoly is that we're in a very small Market the basic lie you tell as a monopoly is that the market you're in is much bigger than it looks

principles.text: Start with a very small market, dominate it, then expand in concentric circles; going after a giant market on day one is a mistake.
principles.quote: you start with a really small market and you take over that whole market and then uh and then over time you find ways to expand that market in in concentric circles

principles.text: Monopolies come from proprietary tech roughly 10x better, network effects, economies of scale and branding.
principles.quote: you want to have a technology that's an order of magnitude better than the next best thing

principles.text: Aim to be the last mover, since most of a company's value lies far in the future; durability matters more than growth rate.
principles.quote: we always overvalue in Silicon Valley is growth rates and we undervalue durability
